script.speaker: Coordinator

script.speaker: Caller
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Coordinator

script.text: What time should I arrive?

script.speaker: Coordinator

script.speaker: Coordinator

sections.title: Open day at the repair yard

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Welcome to the repair yard. The plan shows the junction in the middle. The north edge is at the top of your plan. I will describe the four stops, then tell you how to take part in the afternoon activities.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The sharpening bench is west of the central junction. Follow the left-hand path and look for the low wooden canopy.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The timber store is to the north, straight ahead from the centre towards the top of the plan. The doors will remain open during the tour.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The sorting shed is to the east, on the right-hand side. You can see the sign from the junction before you reach the building.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The demonstration tent is south of the junction, at the bottom of the plan. That is the covered area with room for a group.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Put broken metal fittings in the sorting shed. The timber store holds usable wood and the bench is kept clear for tools.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The short safety talk takes place in the demonstration tent. It is not part of the tour inside the timber store.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Spare wooden strips are available in the timber store, on a low shelf beside the doorway.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: For the practical activity, closed shoes are required. You will be given the other protective items when you arrive.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: You will hear a bell when the first session ends. Finish the action you are doing and put the tool down.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: If you need drinking water, refill your bottle beside the gate before you leave the yard.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: That is the route for today. If a path is busy, wait at the junction until the guide signals that you can move on.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: We need a plan for testing the notices in the learning centre. We agreed to work on how visitors find a room rather than on the colour of the walls.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: All right. Let’s go through the details.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: We should measure the time taken to find a room. We discussed counting how many colours the visitors remember, but it would answer a different question.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: Let’s collect data during the morning. The building hosts a separate event in the evening, and the afternoon class uses the route we need.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: Both routes should start at the entrance. Starting at the stairs would miss the first sign; the desk is not on the second route.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: Dana will print the replacement notices. Robin is doing the checklist, and Leena is only reviewing the data afterwards.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: Robin will prepare the observer checklist. Dana can look at it later, but won’t write the first version.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: Leena has offered to review the data table after both sessions. We will ask her to check how the times have been entered.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: Before the main sessions, we should run a trial with one visitor. A survey of all the staff would take longer and would not test the route.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: Each observer should use a stopwatch for the duration. Start it after giving the same instructions to every visitor.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: Mark the first incorrect turn on a small map. That will show whether people are getting lost at the same place.

script.speaker: Robin
script.text: Give each visitor a number in the notes. The names would not help us compare the routes.

script.speaker: Dana
script.text: We now have a plan we can repeat. After both sessions, we can put the notes together and discuss which comparisons are justified.

sections.title: Looking at paper in a workshop

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today I want to explain how small observations can reveal the structure of a sheet. We will look at how it bends, how it takes up moisture and what can be learned from comparing samples.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A sheet often has a grain. The word describes the direction in which many of the fibres are aligned.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Begin by comparing two gentle bends. A sharp crease is unnecessary and makes it harder to reuse the same piece.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: If you compare two tears, begin from the same edge for each sample so that the positions can be described consistently.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: To see whether the surface takes up moisture quickly, place a small drop of water near the centre. Watch the boundary of the drop.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Measure the spread after the same interval for both papers. A mark taken earlier on one sheet would not be directly comparable.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let both sheets rest in the same room first. This helps reduce differences in starting moisture. It does not make the sheets the same thickness.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A supporting sheet can keep the sample flat while it dries. Use the same arrangement for each sample if you are comparing them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Trace the original outline lightly with a pencil before wetting. You can then see which parts changed position.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Take a photograph from above after the samples dry. The image helps compare the shapes without handling the sheets again.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Finally, write down the room temperature beside the result. Someone repeating the comparison will then know one of its conditions.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Taken together, those observations describe how the sheet behaves. Keep the methods with your results, so another group can repeat the comparison.
